wine.name: Chevalier-Montrachet
wine.classification: Grand Cru of the Côte de Beaune
wine.sites: Chevalier-Montrachet, the grand cru on the steep upper slope directly above Le Montrachet, wholly within Puligny-Montrachet, on thin, stony limestone soil; the vines are farmed biodynamically.
wine.making: Fermented and aged in oak barrels, a modest share of them new, for about a year, then moved to tank for several months more on its lees before it is bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Acacia and lime blossom, white peach and lemon zest over hazelnut and crushed chalk; taut and slow to open, a fine, stony line rather than richness, with a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Closed for its first five to eight years, it opens slowly and keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a wide white Burgundy glass.

records.table: Just above Le Montrachet, on thin and stony soil, Leflaive farms its Chevalier-Montrachet biodynamically and raises it in barrel. Taut, chalky and slow to open, more line than richness, it is a white that gains from air when young.
records.story: Generations of Leflaives had farmed in Puligny, but the domaine took its shape in the early twentieth century, when Joseph Leflaive (1870 to 1953), an engineer, came home to the village after phylloxera and bought vineyards one by one. After his death his sons ran the domaine together, among them Vincent Leflaive (1921 to 1993), and they made its name abroad as the reference for Puligny's precise, stony whites. In 1990 Vincent's daughter, Anne-Claude Leflaive (1956 to 2015), came to share the direction with a cousin and soon led it alone. She began trials of biodynamic farming in the vineyards and by the late 1990s had turned the whole domaine over to it, an early convert among the great domaines of Burgundy. In the early 1990s the domaine added a small parcel of Le Montrachet. Chevalier-Montrachet is the wine it leads with: its parcel sits on the thin, stony upper slope, above the deeper soils of Le Montrachet and Bâtard, and gives a narrower, more chiselled wine than either. Les Pucelles, the premier cru, is the bottle a guest meets more often; the Chevalier is the house's grand cru measure. Its virtues are line and patience, and it asks the same of whoever opens it.

wine.name: Meursault Premier Cru Les Perrières
wine.sites: Les Perrières, on the slope south of the village towards Puligny, above Les Charmes, on stony limestone where stone was once quarried, which gives the climat its name.
wine.making: Fermented and aged in oak barrels in the domaine's deep, cold cellars, with a modest share of new wood, and kept on its lees for well over a year before bottling; the vines are farmed biodynamically.
wine.glass: Lemon, ripe pear and hazelnut over crushed stone and a flinty, smoky note; broad yet taut, with brown butter in the middle and a long line of firm acidity.
wine.ageing: Generous young, it closes for a few years and then keeps for fifteen to twenty.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly; a wide white Burgundy glass.

records.table: Meursault has no grand cru, and Lafon's Meursault Perrières comes from the stony premier cru towards Puligny most often argued for one. Raised in barrel in cold cellars, it is broad yet taut, with hazelnut, ripe pear and a flinty edge, and keeps for twenty years.
records.story: The domaine's founder married into Meursault in the 1890s and gathered vineyards in its well known climats, Perrières, Genevrières and Charmes among them, with a parcel of Le Montrachet and the walled Clos de la Barre around the family house. In 1923 he revived the Paulée de Meursault, the feast that closes the harvest, and later added to it a literary prize paid in bottles of Meursault. After his time the family let most of its vines to sharecroppers, who farmed them for a share of the crop, and the domaine bottled only part of its own wine. In 1984 the founder's great grandson took charge and over the following years brought the vineyards back into the family's own hands; from 1998 he farmed them biodynamically, and in 1999 the family began a second estate in the Mâconnais, the Héritiers du Comte Lafon. Meursault has no grand cru, and Les Perrières, stony ground above Les Charmes, is the premier cru most often argued for promotion. In Lafon's cold cellars it gains breadth without losing its line. Meursault is often sold on richness alone; this wine shows it can be precise as well.

wine.name: Corton-Charlemagne
wine.classification: Grand Cru of the Côte de Beaune
wine.sites: A small parcel of Corton-Charlemagne, the white grand cru on the high, cool upper slopes of the hill of Corton, which spans Aloxe-Corton, Pernand-Vergelesses and Ladoix-Serrigny.
wine.making: Fermented and aged in oak barrels and left long on its lees, which keeps the wine in the reductive, struck match register the domaine is known for; then bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Struck match and flint over lemon oil, white peach and hazelnut skin; tight and cool, with a firm, chalky line and a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Austere for its first five to ten years, it then opens towards hazelnut and honey and keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle so the struck match note can settle; a wide white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The white grand cru of the hill of Corton, its own appellation across three communes.

records.table: Struck match is the mark of Coche-Dury, a Meursault family domaine, and its Corton-Charlemagne carries it from a small parcel of the white grand cru on the hill of Corton. Tight and saline when young, it opens slowly over many years.
records.story: The hill of Corton carries the name of Charlemagne (about 747 to 814), who, the story goes, held vines there, and in 775 gave land on the hill to the abbey of Saulieu. A later legend says white grapes were planted on his part of the slope so that red wine would not stain his beard. The hill's white wine kept his name, and in 1937, when the appellations of the Côte de Beaune were drawn, Corton-Charlemagne became a grand cru spread over three communes, with Corton, the red, below it. Coche-Dury is a small Meursault family domaine whose name joins two families, Coche and Dury, by a marriage of the 1970s. Its wines, from Bourgogne Blanc to the grand cru, are made the same way: long lees ageing in barrel and a deliberate reduction that gives a struck match note over citrus and salt. The style spread far beyond Burgundy, and the domaine passed to the next generation in 2010 without changing it. The Corton-Charlemagne comes from a small parcel and is made in very small quantity. Keep it, and when its time comes, keep a decanter beside it.

wine.sites: The Clos des Ducs, a walled premier cru on the slope beside the village of Volnay, on stony limestone; the vines are farmed biodynamically.

records.table: Held whole by d'Angerville and named, as the story goes, for the Dukes of Burgundy, Clos des Ducs is a walled Volnay premier cru beside the village. Pale, fine and perfumed, Volnay in its silken register, it is served a touch below room temperature.
records.story: The Dukes of Burgundy, the story goes, kept vines at Volnay, and the walled vineyard beside the village took their name. In 1804 a forebear of the family bought the estate, and it passed by descent to the Marquis d'Angerville. In the 1920s the Marquis of the day took on the merchants: he denounced the fraud by which wine from elsewhere was sold as Burgundy, was shut out by the merchants for it, and answered by bottling and selling his own wine at the domaine, among the early growers of the Côte d'Or to do so. His stand fed the appellation laws of the 1930s. His son ran the domaine for half a century until his death in 2003, and the family's own selection of Pinot Noir, known as Pinot d'Angerville, was planted well beyond Volnay. The next generation took charge in 2003, turned the vines to biodynamic farming and in 2012 founded Domaine du Pélican in the Jura. Clos des Ducs is the heart of the domaine: a monopole beside the house, and a Volnay premier cru argued for promotion. In the glass it makes Volnay's case: perfume and line rather than weight.

wine.classification: Premier Cru: a monopole parcel of the house within the climat Les Grèves
wine.sites: A parcel in the heart of Les Grèves, the Beaune premier cru on the middle of the slope, whose name means gravel: pebbly limestone soil that drains well.
wine.making: Fermented in vats and aged in oak barrels, a share of them new, for over a year in the house's cellars before it is bottled by the house.

records.table: Once the vineyard of Beaune's Carmelite nuns, Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus is Bouchard's monopole parcel in the heart of Beaune Grèves. Supple and round, with red cherry and a touch of clove, it is a Beaune premier cru that pours well young.
records.story: A cloth merchant from the Dauphiné founded the house in 1731, settling in Burgundy and turning to wine, and his son began to buy vineyards in the 1770s. Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus belonged then to the Carmelite nuns of Beaune. One of them, Sister Marguerite du Saint-Sacrement (1619 to 1648), was devoted to the Infant Jesus and, the story goes, foretold that Anne of Austria, long childless, would bear a son; the future Louis XIV was born in 1638, and the vineyard took its name from her devotion. The Revolution took it from the convent, and in 1791 the house bought it at the sale of church land. In 1820 Bouchard bought the fifteenth century Château de Beaune, the fortress built for Louis XI, and its bastions have held the house's cellars and its library of old vintages since. In 1995 the house was sold to the Henriot family of Champagne, who also bought Domaine William Fèvre in Chablis three years later. The parcel has stayed whole in the house's hands for more than two centuries. It is a Beaune premier cru of charm, and the story of the nun and the King is the one to tell as it is poured.

questions.q: Bouchard Père et Fils bought Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus at the Revolution. From whom had the land been taken?

The Dukes of Burgundy
The Hospices de Beaune
The monks of Cîteaux
questions.exp: The vineyard was the Carmelite convent's until the Revolution, when church land was sold and the house bought it in 1791; its name recalls a Carmelite's devotion, not the Dukes or Cîteaux.

sources.title: The Sommelier's Codex: the library record of Bouchard Père et Fils
Côte d'Or: A Celebration of the Great Wines of Burgundy

report: No page or search was open to the author or to the refuter: the search budget shared by the run was spent and the network refuses every host, so the record's one https source is the Codex's own library, read in place, as in chunks f2 and f3; the refuter's reading is in reviews/check-f1.json.

From the library or the plan: 1731, the monopole parcel in Grèves named for the Carmelite nuns' devotion, the Château de Beaune of the fifteenth century as the cellars, Clos de la Mousse, Ancienne Cuvée Carnot, La Cabotte, Bouchard Aîné as a separate house.

From the author's reading, unconfirmed here: the founder as a cloth merchant from the Dauphiné, the son's first vineyards in the 1770s, Sister Marguerite du Saint-Sacrement's dates (1619 to 1648) and her prophecy, the purchase of 1791, the Château de Beaune bought in 1820 and built for Louis XI, the sale to the Henriot family in 1995.
The library calls Ancienne Cuvée Carnot a premier cru monopole in Volnay; the author reads it as a named cuvée within Caillerets, so the record says a cuvée, and the refuter should settle it.
The founder (Michel Bouchard) and his son (Joseph Bouchard) are described rather than named, for want of their dates.

changed: others[1]: Clos de la Mousse is no longer the house's other monopole in Beaune, since the house holds more than one there in the refuter's reading; it is now another of them.
questions[1].exp: the claim that the Hospices kept their vineyards at the Revolution was not confirmed and is cut; the explanation now says why the nearest distractors fail.
sources: the Codex's own library, read in place, added as the record's one https source, so the draft passes the lint; the report's draft line now says how the record is sourced.
open: The library calls Ancienne Cuvée Carnot a premier cru monopole in Volnay; the record's cuvée from Caillerets is kept, as the library's own holdings line has it.
